item.title: U.N. watchdog agency pushes for access to key Iran nuclear site
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: The U.N. nuclear watchdog is "increasingly concerned" about Iran refusing its inspectors access to an underground uranium enrichment facility in Isfahan, where highly enriched uranium is thought to be buried, according to Reuters.Iran's chief negotiator told Al Jazeera Thursday that U.S. officials asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to facilitate negotiations between Washington and Tehran. The White House has not responded directly to the report."We don't need a deal with Iran," President Trump declared Thursday, ordering Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic politics instead. Hours earlier, Mr. Trump had again claimed victory in the war, but acknowledged it wasn't over, saying it was "just a question of when we want to end it."

Turkey and Qatar reach a mutual defense agreement
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani signed a mutual defense agreement Friday in Istanbul, according to Erdogan's office.
In a statement posted on X, the office said the two sides would continue working together to prevent the resurgence of war in the Gulf region and "persuade the parties to resolve their problems through diplomacy."
There were no further details on the defense agreement between the countries, which already share deep military ties.
The deal follows a joint defense agreement signed between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August in which the three nations pledged to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. It was not clear if this deal carries the same weight.

item.title: U.S. gave Singapore scant help with Alice Huang probe, source says
item.description:
Singaporean authorities seized the passport of then-Megaspeed chief executive Alice Huang in June 2025 and held it for eight months, preventing her departure while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into advanced Nvidia chips possibly being shipped to China.
One source with knowledge of the matter told CBS News on Friday the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington during the time she was in the Asian city-state. This source said officials in Washington were "not forthcoming" in response to Singapore's requests for help, and no substantive assistance has been provided to date.
Singapore's government confirmed in a statement this week that it reached out to both the U.S. Department of Justice and the FBI for assistance with its investigation.
Alice Huang is the suspected Chinese spy at the center of the extramarital affair scandal that toppled Nvidia founder Jensen Huang from the helm of the global tech giant he built over three decades.
A screengrab from CTI video footage shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, in black, at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, May 22, 2025.
CTI via Reuters TV
Since February 2025, Singaporean authorities have been investigating whether Alice Huang and Megaspeed worked with California-based Supermicro to ship the Silicon Valley firm's computer servers — equipped with advanced Nvidia chips — to China, the source told CBS News.
Alice Huang flew into Singapore in June 2025 for a voluntary interview with Singapore-based investigators from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, according to the source.

item.title: Boy found alive after 6 days lost in wilderness: "Grounded for life"
item.description:
A 17-year-old boy with autism was found alive Thursday after six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands.
The boy, whom police identified only as William, had begun camping with a teenage friend when he disappeared last Friday near Walhalla, a former gold-mining town 185 kilometers (115 miles) east of Melbourne, police said.
A police helicopter crew found him surrounded by wilderness lying asleep on a flat rock beside a creek, and he was later reunited with his mother. William was in good spirits and mostly in good health, the police statement said.
Video shot from the rescue helicopter showed he was shirtless and sunburned. He was wearing shorts and boots and was using towels as blankets.
"I'm just over the moon that he's alive," his mother, Elizabeth, told reporters. The AP has decided not to provide her family name to avoid identifying her son.
"And he's never leaving the house again. He's grounded for life. He's not going anywhere ever again," she joked.
Police video showed Elizabeth embrace her son after the rescue helicopter landed to complete its mission.
William was later taken to a hospital for his health to be monitored, police said.
"Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health," they said in the statement.
In this image made from video and provided by the Victoria State Police 17-year-old William, center right, is embraced by his mother Elizabeth, while in a helicopter in Cowwarr, Australia, Nov. 12, 2026, after William spent six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands.
Victoria Police via AP
William's family have said he has Level 2 autism. That requires "substantial support," according to the Australian advocacy group Autism360.

item.title: Microsoft seeing "continued recovery" amid major worldwide outage
item.description:
From Asia to the U.S., a Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on into a second day, impacting users, companies and government operations around the world.
The outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.
On Friday morning, the Redmond, Washington-based company said it was making "encouraging recovery progress," noting improvements in email delivery. However, users may still experience "intermittent issues" as the company continues its recovery efforts, Microsoft said.
The company apologized to its users on X, saying it "regret[s] the impact these outages had on those who depend on us."
The outage affected Microsoft's suite of business products, as well as those geared toward personal use for individuals, students and families. The Microsoft outage impacted people in 74 countries and territories, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks technology outages.
"Microsoft in a Friday the 13th moment as global outage a [causes] very bad day in Redmond," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives said in an X post Friday. "There will be major questions for MSFT in this global outage."
Trying to get the problem under control
Microsoft said it tried different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using "a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure."
Microsoft updated users about its recovery progress through posts on its Microsoft 365 Status X account.
"We're seeing continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific," the company wrote in a post on Friday at 8:32 a.m. ET. item.title: China warns against new U.S. export controls on computer chips
item.description:
China warned the United States on Friday against imposing additional controls on exports of semiconductors in the wake of the scandal surrounding AI chip giant Nvidia and its now-former CEO Jensen Huang.
China "has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures, which disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serves no party's interests," foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a regular press briefing when asked about calls from U.S. lawmakers to impose more limits on exports of chip equipment to China.
"China and the United States should work together to implement the important consensus reached by their respective heads of state and maintain the stable development of China-U.S. economic and trade relations," Mao said.
Jensen Huang — who resigned Thursday — has admitted to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. They're not related.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with Jensen Huang contributed to a lack of oversight by the federal agency over billions in Nvidia AI chip sales, CBS News has learned. The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.
During an interview on CNBC on Friday morning, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent placed the blame on Lutnick's Commerce Department for not including Megaspeed on what's known as the Entity List, which would restrict their ability to access U.S. technology products.
Bessent said that his department as well as the Defense Department, State Department and U.S. trade representative all supported adding Megaspeed to the list.
"They were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months," Bessent said, before referring to the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. "Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal process...

item.title: Company under scrutiny for ties to Nvidia and China
item.description:
The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. On Thursday, Jensen Huang resigned.
In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.
And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.
Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall.
Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In a statement Thursday, Megaspeed said it "takes its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws extremely seriously" and that it's "committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government."

item.title: Critics say Lutnick failed to cut off diversion of Nvidia chips to China
item.description:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with Nvidia's ousted CEO Jensen Huang contributed to the federal agency's lack of oversight over billions in Nvidia AI chip sales, CBS News has learned.
Before President Trump nominated Lutnick to lead the Commerce Department, Lutnick was the chairman and CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, a New York investment bank which held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time.
Lutnick developed a warm relationship with Huang, who resigned Thursday as reports of a growing number of affairs caused new uncertainty about the world's dominant AI chipmaker. One of Huang's alleged relationships was with Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen Huang), who is believed by the U.S. to be a Chinese spy. She ran Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that became one of Nvidia's biggest customers for AI chips and is suspected of illegally shipping Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to Chinese entities, circumventing a U.S. ban.
As commerce secretary, Lutnick took the helm of an agency responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals.
One way the Commerce Department keeps this information and technology out of the hands of China and other adversaries is by putting foreign companies and individuals on its Entity List. This restricts their ability to access U.S. technology products, and inclusion on the list means that the department believes there's a risk that the entity is involved in activities that are contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.
In 2024, under the Biden administration, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security launched an investigation into Nvidia's chip sales to Megaspeed to determine whether they were being redirected to China. item.title: Star of reality show "Below Deck" arrested after teenager dies
item.description:
A cast member from the U.S. reality TV show "Below Deck" has been arrested in Turkey over a fight in the resort city of Bodrum that left a 17-year-old dead, local media reported Thursday.
Joao Franco, 36, and his brother Carlos allegedly became involved in an altercation with shopkeepers in Bodrum last Saturday evening, according to the private Demiroren News Agency.
Franco, whom the agency identified as a yacht captain, appeared on the Bravo channel's "Below Deck Down Under" and "Below Deck Mediterranean" from 2018, as well as "The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City."
The brothers were intoxicated and an argument broke out when they started swearing, Demiroren reported. During the subsequent fight, teenager Muhammet Koyabakan fell and hit his head on the ground. He suffered a severe head injury and cardiac arrest but was revived at the scene, according to the regional Voices Newspaper.
He was taken to a hospital but died on Monday.
The Franco brothers, who are Portuguese nationals, were detained and later formally arrested.
Joao Franco is seen in "Below Deck Down Under."
Mark Rogers/Bravo via Getty Images
News reports did not specify the charges against them, but Demiroren said they told police they were attacked and acted in self-defense. They denied hitting Koyabakan.
Bodrum, a port city on the Aegean Sea, is a favored spot for wealthy yacht owners. Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos are among the billionaires who have visited in recent years.
"Below Deck" follows the lives of crew members aboard luxury yachts as they interact with each other and their guests. The show premiered on Bravo in 2013.
In his official bio on Bravo, Franco said he has eight years of experience in the yachting industry.

item.title: Man dies after eating bomb disguised as traditional sweet
item.description:
An Indian man died after a crude bomb disguised as a traditional sweet exploded in his mouth, police said Friday.
Some rural communities use the homemade devices to kill wild boars by packing balls of dough with gunpowder, often sourced from firecrackers or quarries. According to the Economic Times, the devices are designed to explode when an animal bites them.
But they also resemble a common Indian dessert called rasgulla, a soft, round sweet soaked in sugar syrup -- and traditionally eaten whole.
The dead man was identified as 35-year-old Rajendra Barautiya.
He was gathered around a bonfire on Tuesday in Dindori district, in the central state of Madhya Pradesh, when a fellow villager brought the "sweet" and another gave it to him.
"The bomb, used by some tribal people in the area to kill wild boars, was offered to this man," police officer Rekha Singh told AFP. "It exploded in his mouth."
Barautiya was rushed to hospital with severe injuries but died.
The villager who handed him the sweet was identified by police as Ramabhagat Barautiya, who described it as a rasgulla, the New Indian Express reported.
A dessert called rasgulla is seen at a Diwali festival at RangMahal Indian Restaurant in Causeway Bay in this undated file photo.
Edmond So/South China Morning Post via Getty Images
"The incident has triggered widespread shock and fear in the village, with residents struggling to comprehend how a casual evening conversation ended in such a tragic manner," the outlet said.
Two men have been arrested and charged with culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
"We don't know if the motive was to kill, or if it was a mischief," Singh added. "That is a matter of investigation."

item.title: Pope Leo calls on followers to "value women" and "respect girls"
item.description: Pope Leo visited Peru on Thursday, where he said he learned "what it means to be a shepherd" when he had lived and served in the country for several decades. He gave an emotional speech in which he denounced the culture of "machismo" and called on followers to "value women." Chris Livesay has more.
